newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark sees 25 pct of its power from gas by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Denmark sees 25 pct of its power from gas by 2000.

text.p: COPENHAGEN, 10 June, Reuter - Natural gas' share in Danish energy use to is set to leap by the end of the century, Povl Asserhoej, executive vice president of Danish Oil and Natural Gas company (DONG) said on Tuesday.
Natural gas has taken 19 percent of Denmark's energy market, an increase from just one percent in 1984, and the share is set to rise to 25 percent by 2000, Asserhoej told a news conference.
Oil's share in the energy balance has lost correspondingly.

Asserhoej said that in 1972, when Denmark's natural gas industry started, imported oil accounted for 92 percent of all energy consumption. But following the first energy crisis of 1973, the decision was taken to reduce this dependence.
By 1984, oil use was down to 55 percent, with coal use jumping to 39 percent.
But the current plan is to reduce coal and oil use in favour of natural gas and renewable energy.

DONG projections show oil accounting for 42 percent of the total balance in 2000, with coal taking a 22 percent share, gas up to 25 percent, and renewables, particularly wind power, providing 11 percent.
Svend Auken, environment and energy minister, said Denmark's energy policy was based on security of supply, energy efficiency and environmental protection.

"In these times of energy glut, we forget that the reason most countries have an energy policy is security of supply," said Auken. He added that Denmark diversified away from oil precisely because of that concern but the same worries are now being felt over dependence on imported natural gas.

Apart from relatively small volumes from Britain, the Netherlands and Denmark itself, Auken said that in the future all Europe's gas will come from "our Norwegian brothers, our Russian comrades, and our Algerian friends. That is not a situation without difficulty."
Even so, Auken said that gas' share of the energy balance may rise to 40 percent eventually.
He also had ambitious plans for renewable energy, especially wind power.

"In future we hope it will account for 35 percent of the balance," he said. "It's not only environmentally sound, it's also economically sound - one of the main Danish exports is wind energy and windmills."
But for the time being, coal remained the biggest provider of Danish electricity, accunting for 80 percent of the total.
Auken said he planned to run down coal's role, depite his claim that Denmark has the cheapest and most efficient coal generating plants in the world.
